one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent created an inspect.py file that shadowed Python's standard library inspect module, then misdiagnosed the resulting import failures as numpy/scipy version incompatibilities, cycling through multiple broken dependency states before producing a solution.txt whose objective value does not satisfy the evaluator's threshold.
t_err_evidence: Step 5: agent creates /app/inspect.py via heredoc; this file imports numpy and shadows the stdlib inspect module, which is later referenced by numpy.ma.core (inspect.cleandoc). The agent proceeds without verifying whether the filename conflicts with any stdlib module.
t_commit_evidence: Step 11: after seeing the inspect.cleandoc AttributeError (step 8), the agent misattributes the failure to a numpy/scipy version incompatibility and runs 'pip install -U scipy'. From this point the agent is locked into a sequence of wrong dependency manipulations (downgrading numpy to 1.26.4 at step 18, scipy to 1.14.0 at step 19, then further to numpy 1.23.5 at step 39), each introducing new incompatibilities. Even after renaming inspect.py at step 27, the downgraded scipy/numpy combination causes SLSQP and trust-constr to fail (steps 30, 32, 44), preventing a clean solver run.
t_surface_evidence: Step 8: running solve.py prints the p/q stats from inspect.py (unexpected output proving the shadowing) and then crashes with 'AttributeError: module inspect has no attribute cleandoc', which is the first observable failure signal.
trigger_explanation: The agent created the data-inspection script and named it inspect.py without checking whether that filename conflicts with any Python standard library module. No verification step was taken before writing the file.
forewarning_evidence: Step 8 output shows both (a) unexpected p/q statistics printed at the start of solve.py execution (indicating inspect.py is being imported as a side effect) and (b) the AttributeError traceback originating from /app/inspect.py, signaling that a local file is shadowing the stdlib. Steps 9 and 10 repeat the same pattern with unexpected p/q prints prefixed to the errors.
